[Financial News] Goldman Sachs lowered its 12-month KOSPI target from 9,000 to 7,500. The move came about three weeks after it cut the target from 12,000 to 9,000 on the 25th of last month. This is thought to reflect increased volatility in the domestic stock market in the second half and a slowdown in the pace of upward earnings estimate revisions. Goldman Sachs nevertheless maintained its overweight recommendation, saying that the Korean stock market had the greatest upside potential among Asian markets.
 12,000→9,000→7,500... down 37.5% in five months 
 According to Investing.com and other outlets, Goldman Sachs set its 12-month KOSPI target at 7,500 in a report on the 17th (local time), 16.7% below its previous target. That is 37.5% below the June peak of 12,000.
 Goldman Sachs raised its KOSPI target to 12,000 on June 3 and kept it there despite a sharp decline in AI-related stocks in the second half. It then cut the target to 9,000 on the 25th of last month before lowering it once again.
 Goldman Sachs said in its report that despite the Korean stock market’s strong returns in the first half, the market had been hesitant to fully reflect corporate fundamentals in stock prices. It assessed that the second half had been difficult, with high volatility and a slowdown in momentum behind upward earnings forecast revisions.
 “Reflecting a 70% Drop in Memory Earnings”... “Excessive Despite Being Sold Out Through 2029” 
 Goldman Sachs believes that although it lowered its target, current stock prices are excessively pessimistic. It said stock prices in the memory sector already reflect a scenario in which next year’s consensus earnings fall by 70%, and called that excessive.
 The target is based on conservative valuation assumptions, but expected returns remain high. Goldman Sachs forecasts a 50% total return in dollar terms over the next 12 months. Based on the KOSPI’s close of 5,067.44 on the 18th, that implies about 48% upside to 7,500.
 By sector, Goldman Sachs saw attractive opportunities in non-memory stocks, whose valuations had fallen to historic lows. The 2027 annual general meeting season and expanded shareholder returns were cited as additional catalysts for gains. It also forecast that next year’s supply-demand conditions would be favorable, thanks to large-scale share buybacks and light investor positioning, and said the market had yet to fully reflect the gains from improvements in corporate governance in stock prices.
